doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Bass player who sings: cabaret and recording vocals separately
summary: She is a bass player who sings; cabaret focuses on the song and audience, and in the studio engineers make her record bass and vocals separately.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Right. Yeah, that’s funny. So are you a bass player who sings, or are you a singer who plays the bass?

I’m a bass player that sings. You know I recently did a cabaret show where it was more about the singing. In fact I was being directed by this director of this cabaret show who had me put down the bass and sit on a stool and sing some songs. And that to me was © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
more about the singing. But if you think about the cabaret role, the cabaret role is someone singing, that’s what the focus is on.

Sometimes only just with a piano player. Do you know what I mean? The cabaret, this is where I think the cabaret is different maybe from jazz, it’s much more about the song and talking to the audience and connecting there, which was good discipline for me, to have to be there, to that extreme. I sometimes think if I’m going to do a cabaret show I still want to shift it a bit more towards jazz, Do you know what I mean? I still want to do instrumentals. I still want to keep the focus on instrumental jazz peppered with some nice tunes. So for me it’s hard to do a whole cabaret show.
Is there a thing about just feeling more exposed to the audience if it’s just you and the microphone? You know when you have a bass you’ve got this other thing.

Yeah I know, and I have had people say to me over the years you should just really put the bass down. I don’t know look at Esperanza Spaulding, you know, a good example. She is out there playing and singing, and now she is really doing a whole lot of different stuff. I’m not caught up on her latest material but you know, she’s doing it in her way. It’s very interesting, but she’s playing and singing. And honestly I’m feeling now that the bass lines I’m playing when I play the bass actually dictates how I sing so I really have to separate the two when I’m in the studio because they don’t like the leaking and they don’t like this and they want —

If you’ve got the vocals then they don’t want the bass leaking into that, so in the studio, so far, I’ve done everything separate. It’s not really by choice it’s just because the engineers want to do it that way, or the producer. I’ve done four Japanese records and they’ve all been done that way, and they’re all vocals on every track. So it’s a lot of work. It’s okay, because then there’s a discipline on doing a couple of takes vocally until you’re really in the song you know. But you know, I prefer live, where you sing and you play at the same time.
